work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Transient gap-junction blockade makes planarian fragments build heads of other species
statement: Temporary exposure of planarian fragments to a blocker of electrical synapses (gap junctions) causes them to build head shapes of other planarian species 100–150 million years distant, with no genetic change; Levin interprets this as the bioelectric network navigating to other attractors in morphospace, and the worms later remodel back to normal.
quote: One example of this plasticity of morphogenetic behavior (expanding on the default genetically encoded repertoire) is the fact that temporary exposure to a blocker of electrical synapses (i.e., an anesthetic) causes planarian fragments to create the heads of other species, with no genetic change required (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015; Sullivan et al. 2016).
scope: Planarian flatworms (Girardia dorotocephala and related species), author's lab (Emmons-Bell et al. 2015)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Newt kidney tubules keep normal diameter with fewer, larger cells, down to one cell
statement: In newts whose embryonic cells are made larger (e.g. by polyploidy), kidney tubules use fewer cells to keep the normal tubule diameter and body size, and with enormous cells a single cell bends around itself to form the tubule, showing that different molecular mechanisms are called on to reach the same large-scale anatomical goal.
quote: However, if the cells of the early embryo are artificially made to be larger, fewer cells will be used, resulting in the same (normal) tubule diameter and overall body size. Remarkably, this can be pushed to a fascinating extreme: if the cells are made to be enormous, a single cell will bend around itself, producing the normal size tubule diameter.
scope: Polyploid newt embryos (Fankhauser 1945)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Xenobots perform kinematic self-replication not known in any other species
statement: Xenobots, proto-organisms that form spontaneously from dissociated frog embryo skin cells, are motile via cilia and perform kinematic self-replication, building copies of themselves from loose cells in the medium, a novel solution reached within 48 h without any evolutionary history of selection as Xenobots.
quote: The most remarkable novel behavior is that of kinematic self-replication: Xenobots build copies of themselves by rearranging loose cells provided to them in the medium. This is Von Neumann-style replication that is not, to our knowledge, used by any other species on Earth.
scope: Xenobots made from Xenopus laevis embryonic ectoderm (Kriegman et al. 2021a)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Scrambled Xenopus tadpole faces reach a normal frog face by new paths
statement: During metamorphosis, Xenopus laevis tadpoles reach the correct frog face configuration not only from a normal tadpole configuration but also from a wide range of experimentally scrambled craniofacial configurations, using new paths through morphospace that end in the same goal region.
quote: For example, during metamorphosis, the tadpole of Xenopus laevis can reach the correct frog face region of morphospace not only from its default starting position (a normal tadpole configuration), but also from a wide range of scrambled configurations (Vandenberg et al. 2012)—using new paths through that morphospace that nevertheless end up in the same goal region (Friston et al. 2015; Pezzulo and Levin 2016).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with induced craniofacial malformations (author's lab, Vandenberg et al. 2012)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: A few bioelectrically induced lens cells recruit host cells to build a normal-sized lens
statement: When an ectopic lens is induced in tail tissue by bioelectric modulation, misexpressing the ion channel in only a small subset of the needed cells suffices: these cells recruit unmodified host cells to reach the critical mass for a normal-sized lens, so downstream modules such as size control are activated without micromanagement.
quote: For example, when an ectopic lens (in tail tissue) is induced by bioelectric modulation, it is sufficient to misexpress the channel only in a small subset of the needed cells: once their organ-level goal is specified, these cells will secondarily recruit other (un-modified) host cells as needed to achieve the critical mass needed to produce a normal-sized lens.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos with ion channel misexpression in tail tissue

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Gap junctions wipe ownership of memory molecules, partly erasing cell individuality
statement: By directly connecting the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells, gap junctions provide an 'owner wiping property' for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience (e.g. calcium flux), so cells cannot tell whether such a signal is their own or a neighbour's; this partly erases individual cell identity and lets the collective scale up measurements, stored goals and actions.
quote: Second, by providing direct connections between the intracellular milieus of cells, they provide an “owner wiping property” for stress signals and other molecular traces of experience: cells cannot tell whether a given memory molecule (e.g., calcium flux) belongs to itself or its neighbors.
scope: Gap-junction-coupled cells in morphogenetic and neural tissues

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Single adult human lung cells self-construct into motile multicellular biobots
statement: A single normal human bronchial epithelial cell from adult lung, cultured in extracellular matrix for two weeks and then transferred to a low-viscosity medium, self-constructs into a multicellular, motile spheroid (an Anthrobot) without genetic editing, scaffolds or manual sculpting.
quote: Each Anthrobot begins as a single cell, derived from the adult human lung, and self‐constructs into a multicellular motile biobot after being cultured in extra cellular matrix for 2 weeks and transferred into a minimally viscous habitat.
scope: Normal human bronchial epithelial (NHBE) progenitor cells from adult donors, in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Morphogenetic plasticity is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cells
statement: The ability of adult, somatic, genetically wild-type human cells to form a novel functional anatomy with new behaviours shows that the plasticity seen in Xenobots is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cells, and is a fundamental feature of wild-type cells that needs no direct genetic manipulation to unlock.
quote: The ability of adult, somatic, human cells to form a novel functional anatomy, with unique behaviors, reveals that this plasticity is not restricted to amphibian or embryonic cell properties, and is a fundamental feature of wild‐type cells that requires no direct genetic manipulation to unlock.
scope: Genetically wild-type cells generally, generalized from adult human airway epithelium and Xenopus embryonic cells

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Lower viscosity may drive apical-out polarity reversal of airway spheroids
statement: The authors hypothesize that airway spheroids keep cilia in the lumen because basal cells interact with the surrounding high-viscosity matrix, and that moving spheroids to a lower-viscosity, water-based medium may trigger basal cells to migrate inward so the ciliated apical layer takes their place on the spheroid surface.
quote: Given that cilia naturally localize into the lumen due to the basal cells’ interaction with the surrounding high‐viscosity matrix, we hypothesized that changing the culture environment to a lower viscosity level (e.g., water‐based media instead of gel‐based matrix) may trigger the basal layer cells to migrate inward and allow the apical layer to take their place on the spheroid cortex.
scope: Human bronchial epithelial spheroids grown in Matrigel and transferred to low-adhesive liquid culture

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Apical-in spheroids become motile within a week in low-adhesive liquid culture
statement: Human bronchial epithelial spheroids that are apical-in and non-motile on release from Matrigel become motile by day 7 in low-adhesive liquid culture, with beating cilia on their outer surface; immunostaining shows a large increase in external multiciliated cells between day 0 and day 7.
quote: This new approach has enabled the originally apical‐in spheroids (that show no motility on day 0 as shown on Figure 1b.1) to became motile by day 7 (Figure 1b.2), featuring highly motile ciliary appendages on the spheroid surface.
scope: NHBE-derived spheroids in vitro, Anthrobot protocol with retinoic acid

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Higher culture viscosity reduces Anthrobot motility and size
statement: Culturing Anthrobots in environments more viscous than the protocol baseline decreases both their motility and their size, suggesting that low-viscosity environments favour the growth of functional, larger bots.
quote: We observed that culture environments with higher viscosity levels than the protocol baseline result in decreased motility (Figure S2, Supporting Information) and size (Figure S3, Supporting Information), suggesting that low‐viscosity environments better facilitate the growth of functional bots as well as yield larger bots.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Initial cell seeding density is a control knob for Anthrobot size and maturation
statement: Changing the initial seeding density of bronchial epithelial cells in Matrigel (half, default or double 30,000 cells/mL) significantly changes the resulting Anthrobot sizes and the time course of motility, though not linearly, suggesting that seeding density is a tractable control parameter for Anthrobot morphology and function.
quote: These results show that the size and time course of maturation of motile bots could be modulated by altering the concentration of cells in the Anthrobot differentiation culture, suggesting initial cell seeding density to be a tractable control knob for Anthrobot morphology and function.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro, seeding densities 15,000–60,000 cells/mL

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobot motility onset follows a sigmoidal time course peaking around day 10
statement: After release from the matrix, the number of motile Anthrobots rises along a sigmoidal curve over three weeks, with the largest change in motility on day 10, and this rise reflects a morphological reorganization that exposes cilia on the surface.
quote: To characterize the temporal dynamics of motility initiation, we periodically (every other day) counted the number of motile spheroids for 3 weeks following dissolution and observed a sigmoidal motility profile with peak change in motility on day 10 (Figure 1C).
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro, first 3 weeks after matrix dissolution

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobot motility is cilia-driven
statement: Blocking ciliary motion with ciliobrevin sharply decreases Anthrobot motility, showing that their locomotion is driven by surface cilia.
quote: We administered the efficient blocker of cilia motion, ciliobrevin,[ 20 ] and observed the expected drastic decrease in motility (See Figure S6, Supporting Information), confirming that the motility of Anthrobots is cilia‐driven.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobot trajectories fall into four movement types
statement: Unsupervised clustering of 30-second trajectory segments from about 200 Anthrobots, described by straightness and gyration indices, yields four statistically distinct movement types: circular, linear, curvilinear and eclectic.
quote: Further investigation of these clusters reveals that each represents a distinct movement type: circular, linear, curvilinear and “eclectic” (Figure 2D).
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in low-adhesive dishes, 5-hour time-lapse tracking

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Circular motion is the most stable Anthrobot behaviour; eclectic motion is transient
statement: In a Markov-chain model of transitions between movement types, circular motion is the most persistent Anthrobot behaviour, followed by linear and curvilinear motion, while eclectic motion acts as a transient intermediate that probabilistically resolves into one of the other three types.
quote: We observed that the most stable movement pattern for an Anthrobot is circular motion, followed by linear/curvilinear motion. The eclectics act more like an intermediate and over time, at least probabilistically, resolve into one of the 3 other categories.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots, 30 s trajectory segments over 5 h

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobots self-organize into discrete, stable movement types with individual fingerprints
statement: Because Anthrobot movement types are highly consistent and rarely interconvert (for example between circular and linear), the authors conclude that Anthrobots self-organize into discrete, stable movement types, each bot having a distinct motility fingerprint.
quote: The fact that Anthrobots exhibit movement types with high “consistency” and low rates of inter‐type conversion (e.g., between circulars and linear) suggests that Anthrobots self‐organize into discrete and stable movement types, each bot having a distinct motility fingerprint.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Morphotype 2 is most ciliated; morphotype 3 has the most polarized cilia
statement: Among the three Anthrobot morphotypes, morphotype 2 (the largest and least regular) is significantly more ciliated than the other two, and morphotype 3 has a significantly more polarized, clustered cilia distribution with the fewest isolated cilia patches.
quote: These four indices together describe type 2 bots as being significantly more ciliated than type 1 and type 3 bots, and type 3 bots as having a significantly more polarized cilia distribution pattern (with the least amount of extra‐cluster noise) in comparison to type 1 and type 2 bots (Figure 3D).
scope: About 350 NHBE-derived Anthrobots

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobots form three morphotypes, split first by size and shape, then by cilia pattern
statement: Principal component analysis and clustering of eight shape and cilia indices from about 350 Anthrobots yields three morphotypes, organized as a decision tree in which size and shape smoothness separate small, smooth spherical bots (morphotype 1) from larger, irregular bots, which are then split by cilia pattern into non-polarized (morphotype 2) and polarized (morphotype 3).
quote: In summary, our morphological characterization pipeline suggest that Anthrobots self‐organize into 3 major morphotypes (Figure 3E) and this relationship can be represented by a developmental decision tree shown on Figure 3F wherein the first “decision point” determines the Anthrobot size and shape.
scope: About 350 NHBE-derived Anthrobots imaged by confocal microscopy

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Non-movers, linear and circular bots map onto morphotypes 1, 2 and 3
statement: Anthrobot behaviour and morphology are significantly associated: non-moving bots fall mostly in morphotype 1 (small, smooth, spherical), linear movers mostly in morphotype 2 (large, non-polarized cilia) and circular movers mostly in morphotype 3 (polarized cilia), and no displacing bot was found in morphotype 1.
quote: We have further computed the statistical significance of these overlaps (using the Fisher test, see Materials and Methods) and conclude that the non‐movers, linear, and circulars significantly correspond with the morphotypes 1, 2 and 3, respectively.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots; 350 imaged bots of which 28 had assigned displacing movement types

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Spherical bots with uniform cilia may not move because ciliary forces cancel
statement: Morphotype 1 Anthrobots are likely non-movers or stationary wigglers, which the authors suggest may be because their radially symmetric spherical shape with evenly distributed cilia makes ciliary propulsion forces cancel out, with small imbalances producing only wiggling.
quote: This may be attributable to their spherical shape with homogeneously distributed cilia where the propulsion forces generated by the ciliary motion are more prone to canceling each other out due to the radially symmetric spherical shape, resulting in little or no movement.
scope: Small, spherical, uniformly ciliated Anthrobots (morphotype 1)

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Linear-moving Anthrobots are more bilaterally symmetric about their movement axis
statement: Linear-moving Anthrobots show higher bilateral symmetry of cilia distribution about their axis of movement than circular movers; for circular bots, but not linear bots, the 90-degree rotated axis is more symmetric than the movement axis (p = 0.048), supporting distinct local symmetry profiles for distinct movement types.
quote: Taken together, these findings support our hypothesis that Anthrobots with distinct movement types have distinct local bilateral symmetry profiles, with linear bots showing higher bilateral symmetry.
scope: 28 displacing NHBE-derived Anthrobots (15 circular, 13 linear)

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobots recapitulate the bilateral symmetry of many wild-type species
statement: The link between straight-line movement and bilateral symmetry in Anthrobots suggests that these synthetic forms, self-assembling in a symmetrical environment, recapitulate a fundamental morphological property seen in many wild-type species and could be used to study how embryos establish a single body midplane.
quote: This suggests that these synthetic forms recapitulate a fundamental morphological property observed in many wild‐type species.
scope: Anthrobots compared with bilaterally symmetric animals

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Faster and more rotational Anthrobots cover more of a neuronal scratch
statement: Anthrobots can move across scratches in human neuronal monolayers in vitro, and bots with higher rotational tendency or higher speed cover a larger proportion of unique positions along the scratch interface.
quote: Taken together, these data reveal that Anthrobots are capable of efficiently moving across damaged tissues, and that bots that have a higher rotational tendency and or higher speed have higher degrees of unique coordinate coverage by moving across a higher percentage of the scratch interface.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in scratched monolayers of hiNSC-derived human neurons, n = 17 bots

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: An intermediate gyration maximizes how closely Anthrobots track scratch edges
statement: In a constrained set of 13 Anthrobots in neuronal scratches, gyration (rotational tendency) has a quadratic relationship with how closely a bot's trajectory follows the scratch edge (p = 0.006), suggesting an intermediate gyration range maximizes edge tracking.
quote: With our constrained dataset, we saw that gyration had a quadratic effect on scratch‐trajectory similarity (Figure 5E) with p = 0.006, suggesting that there is a specific range for gyration where the scratch‐trajectory correlation can be maximized
scope: 13 NHBE-derived Anthrobots with rotational tendency 0.33–0.7 in hiNSC-derived neuronal scratches

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Superbot bridges induce neuronal gap closure in scratched monolayers
statement: Fused Anthrobot assemblies (superbots) placed across a scratch in a human neuronal monolayer induce substantial regrowth of neuronal tissue beneath them within 72 hours, forming a stitch that connects the two sides of the scratch.
quote: Strikingly, within the next 72 h upon inoculation of the superbot into the tissue scratch on day 0, we observed a substantial regrowth of the native tissue taking place (i.e., gap closure), resulting in the formation of a stitch right underneath the “superbot bridge,” connecting the two sides of the scratch (Figure 6B).
scope: Superbots of fused NHBE-derived Anthrobots on scratched hiNSC-derived human neuronal monolayers in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Superbot-induced gap closure is local and restores native tissue density
statement: Neuronal gap closure occurs only at the site where a superbot is placed; the neuronal coverage density there is statistically indistinguishable from intact tissue outside the scratch, while adjacent and distant parts of the scratch have significantly lower coverage.
quote: Thus, the density of the induced gap closure area that formed as a result of the presence of the superbot represented full (statistically indistinguishable from 100%) recovery of the original tissue and was uniquely different from the surrounding scratch area.
scope: Superbots on scratched hiNSC-derived human neuronal monolayers; bridges maintained over 3 days (5 of 10)

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Passive mechanical loading does not reproduce Anthrobot-induced neural repair
statement: Placing a piece of agarose on neuronal scratches for 4 days to provide passive mechanical loading induces no repair, indicating that simple mechanical contact is not sufficient for the gap closure seen with Anthrobot superbots.
quote: Finally, in order to test whether simple (passive) mechanical contact was sufficient to induce the same effect, we incubated neuronal scratches for 4 days with a piece of agarose on top to provide mechanical loading; this induced no repair (see Figure S11, Supporting Information).
scope: Scratched hiNSC-derived human neuronal monolayers in vitro

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobots and Xenobots share similar movement types and transition profiles
statement: Anthrobots and Xenobots both show discrete movement types with very low interconversion between linear and circular motion (0.2% and 0.3% for Anthrobots, 0.5% and 1.6% for Xenobots) and highly consistent circular behaviour (92% and 95%), though Anthrobot linear behaviour is more consistent (80% versus 67%).
quote: The interconversion between linear and circular is very small for Xenobots (0.5% and 1.6%) and Anthrobots (0.2% and 0.3%), while their consistency of Circular behavior is extremely high for Xenobots (95%) just like for Anthrobots (92%).
scope: Human NHBE-derived Anthrobots compared with Xenopus laevis Xenobots

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Similar forms from divergent genomes point to generic laws of morphogenesis
statement: Because Anthrobots and Xenobots, despite highly divergent genomes, ages and tissue origins, assemble into very similar kinds of motile constructs, the authors conclude that generic laws of morphogenesis matter in addition to species-specific genomic information.
quote: Despite their highly divergent genome, age, and tissue origin, the two platforms assemble into very similar types of creatures, illustrating the importance of generic laws of morphogenesis[ 31 ] in addition to species‐specific genomic information.
scope: Self-assembling multicellular constructs from human and amphibian cells

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Superbot size is set by bot number and fusion requires exposed basal layers
statement: Anthrobots fuse into larger superbots only in the days immediately after release from the matrix, while their basal layers are still exposed and can mediate bot-to-bot fusion, and superbot size can be controlled by the number of Anthrobots cultured together in a well.
quote: The tendency of the bots to fuse together and thus form different sized collectives (i.e., superbots) for different scratches can be controlled by modulating the number of Anthrobots cultured together in the same well for fusion, which happens only on days immediately following dissolution while the Anthrobot basal layers are still exposed and thus can mediate the bot‐to‐bot fusion.
scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in the days after matrix dissolution

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Tracheal cells healing neural tissue could not be predicted from current models
statement: That wild-type cells from the trachea move over and heal neural tissue is unexpected given their normal role in the body and could not be predicted from any current molecular or tissue-level model, which suggests screening engineered tissue interactions to uncover novel cell capabilities.
quote: The finding is unexpected given these tissues’ normal roles in the human body – the fact that wild‐type cells from trachea will move over and heal neural tissues could not be predicted from any current molecular or tissue‐level models.
scope: Human airway epithelium-derived Anthrobots interacting with neural tissue

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Patient-derived Anthrobots could be deployed in vivo without an immune response
statement: Because Anthrobots are made from adult human tissue, they could in future be personalized for each patient and deployed in that patient's body without triggering an immune response.
quote: Anthrobots are derived from adult human tissue, and in the future could be personalized for each patient, enabling safe in‐vivo deployment of these robots in the human body without triggering an immune response.
scope: Autologous Anthrobots in human patients

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: Anthrobots may be made from other ciliated human cells such as oviduct or ependyma
statement: Anthrobots may be generable from other ciliated human cells, such as oviductal epithelium or brain ependymal cells, and non-ciliated cell types could be used for bots that need no autonomous motility.
quote: Anthrobots may be able to be generated from other ciliated cells in the human body (e.g., oviductal epithelia or brain ependymal cells), and other cell types can be used for bots when autonomous motility is not needed
scope: Ciliated and non-ciliated adult human cell types

work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
label: One genome yielding diverse forms in different environments could shape evolution
statement: The additional morphogenetic competencies revealed by Anthrobots could matter for evolutionary developmental biology, since the evolution of anatomical and functional features could be affected by the ability of the same genome to produce very diverse forms in different environments.
quote: More fundamentally, these data reveal additional morphogenetic competencies of cells which could have implications for evolutionary developmental biology, as evolution of anatomical and functional features could be affected by the ability of the same genome to produce very diverse forms in different environments.
scope: Evolution of anatomy in multicellular organisms

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: A collective's perceptual field and ability to find alternative paths grow with its size
statement: Extending William James' definition of intelligence (reaching the same goal by different means) to collectives via the perceptual field, the region of space and time an agent can survey for alternative paths to a goal, the authors propose that as a collective grows its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
quote: As the size of a collective increases its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
scope: Cell collectives and other biological collectives

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Neural unification into a self is a pivot of earlier morphogenetic cell communication
statement: It has been hypothesized, and the authors adopt, that the ability of neurons to unify into a centralized self is an evolutionary pivot of earlier cell-communication strategies that first solved problems in anatomical morphospace, a domain also requiring information processing above the single-cell level.
quote: Indeed it has been hypothesized that the remarkable ability of neurons to unify toward a centralized self – the emergent agent that is the subject of memories, preferences, and goals which are not assignable to any of the individual components – is an evolutionary pivot of far earlier cell communication strategies that first solved problems in navigating another domain that requires information processing above the single cell level: anatomical morphospace70.
scope: Evolution of nervous systems from non-neural bioelectric signalling in metazoans

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: The number of embryos a blastoderm forms is not fixed by genetics
statement: The number of individuals formed by an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at one by the genome: temporarily introducing breaks that informationally isolate islands of cells yields twins, triplets and so on, showing the blastoderm is an excitable medium in which several coherent embryos can self-organize.
quote: Indeed, the question of how many individuals are present in an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at 1 by the genetics, because temporary introduction of breaks in the blastoderm (leading to informational isolation of islands of cell masses) results in twins, triplets, etc103.
scope: Early vertebrate (e.g. avian) blastoderms

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Keratocyte fragments migrate to the anode while whole keratocytes migrate to the cathode
statement: In an electric field, whole keratocytes migrate toward the cathode while fragments of keratocytes migrate toward the anode, so the collective (an intact cell) has the opposite taxis to its parts, illustrating that collective behaviour can be a hard-to-predict function of component tendencies.
quote: In an electric field, keratocytes migrate to the cathode, but fragments of keratocytes migrate to the anode104.
scope: Fish keratocytes and keratocyte fragments in applied electric fields

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Targeting instructor-cell voltage converts tadpole melanocytes to a melanoma-like state
statement: In Xenopus tadpoles, briefly targeting the bioelectric state of a small population of instructor cells (with a chloride channel activator or a GlyCl mutant), in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes or DNA damage, converts melanocytes throughout the animal, including distant ones, into an over-proliferative, invasive melanoma-like phenotype via disruption of serotonergic signalling.
quote: This could be achieved in the absence of classical carcinogens, oncogenes, or DNA damage, by brief exposure to chemical (chloride ion channel activator drug) or molecular-genetic (GlyCl mutant) targeting of the bioelectric state of a specific cell population: instructor cells which normally keep the melanocytes in their healthy state via serotonergic signaling118.
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Melanocyte conversion is all-or-none per animal, stochastic only across the cohort
statement: Melanocyte conversion after instructor-cell depolarization is a collective, all-or-none decision: different reagents give different incidences in a cohort (e.g. 70% converted), but each animal is either fully converted or fully normal; a computational model fitted to these incidences predicted interventions (two drugs and a dominant-negative construct) that were then confirmed to produce the first partially converted animals.
quote: Using different reagents could induce different incidences of hyperpigmentation (conversion) in a cohort of animals, but this was a population-level phenotype: for example, 70% of the animals could be converted, but any given animal was either fully converted or fully normal (Fig. 4a, b).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with perturbed instructor-cell bioelectric signalling

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Head-versus-tail choice at a planarian cut cannot be made locally
statement: When a planarian is cut once, cells that were adjacent neighbours at the same positional-information value make a head on one side and a tail on the other, so this anatomical decision cannot be made locally: wound cells must coordinate with the rest of the fragment to learn where they are, which way they face and what structures remain.
quote: In other words, it is actually impossible for an anatomical decision like this to be made locally – the cells of the wound must coordinate with the remaining fragment to get information about where they are located, which way they are facing, and what other structures exist121,122, in order to make adaptive decisions about large-scale growth and form that enable regeneration of normal worms.
scope: Regenerating planarian fragments

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Cryptic planaria randomize head number per animal, not per cell
statement: Perturbing the planarian bioelectric control circuit produces 'Cryptic' destabilized worms whose fragments, even from the same parent, regenerate one-headed and two-headed forms at a set frequency of about 1:2, yet each animal has clear heads and tails rather than mixed tissue, so the randomized bioelectric state is interpreted by collectives rather than by individual cells.
quote: More specifically, several perturbations targeting the bioelectric control circuit (Fig. 5e) have shown randomization of outcome: such Cryptic planaria are destabilized, and fragments (even from the same parent worm) will form 1-head and 2-head forms at a set frequency of ~1:2130 (Fig. 5f).
scope: Planarians after gap-junction or bioelectric perturbation

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Left-right randomization is concordant within an embryo except after VANGL knockdown
statement: Bioelectric and biochemical perturbations of vertebrate left-right patterning randomize laterality only at the level of whole embryos (each embryo's cells agree on L and R identity); the only known perturbation that breaks this concordance is down-regulation of planar-polarity VANGL signalling, which produces speckled L/R marker expression on both sides of the midline.
quote: In all of the many studies on perturbation of the LR pathway, we are aware of only one that actually breaks the concordance: disruption of the planar polarity pathway by down-regulating VANGL signaling149 leads to a speckling on both sides of the midline, consistent with individual cells within a single lateral domain disagreeing on whether they should have L or R identity (Fig. 6a–d).
scope: Vertebrate embryos (chick, Xenopus and others) with perturbed left-right pathways

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Grafted groups of neural crest cells keep their identity; single grafted cells do not
statement: Single neural crest cells transposed to a different anterior-posterior axial domain change their gene expression to match their neighbours, whereas groups of transposed cells keep their original gene expression, which the authors interpret as collectives having greater positional memory (a perceptual field extending further into the past) than individual cells.
quote: Individual cells transposed from one anterior-posterior axial domain to another will change their gene expression to match their neighbors159,161,162. In contrast, groups of cells transposed along the anterior-posterior axis maintain their original gene expression, thus resisting the inductive effects of the surrounding tissue159,161,162.
scope: Vertebrate neural crest (chick, mouse) transplantation

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: The segmentation clock needs a cell collective to oscillate and entrains grafted cells
statement: The vertebrate segmentation clock depends on collectivity: presomitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured individually but resume oscillating when cultured together, wild-type cells grafted into non-cycling mutant fish express her1 without cycling, and cells grafted into tissue at a different clock phase synchronize to their neighbours' phase.
quote: Similarly, pre-somitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured independently, but will resume oscillating when cultured collectively169.
scope: Vertebrate presomitic mesoderm (zebrafish, chick, mouse)

work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
label: Frog embryo brain gene expression is driven by voltage differences, not absolute values
statement: In the frog embryo brain, downstream gene expression is driven by the spatial difference in membrane voltage between regions rather than the absolute voltage of any cells, so cells must read patterns over whole cell fields: collectivity appears in the input as well as the output of cell-group behaviour.
quote: For example, in the frog embryo brain, it is the spatial difference in voltage between regions that drives downstream gene expression, not the absolute value of any cells186,187.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic brain patterning

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Biological memory preserves salience rather than fidelity
statement: Levin proposes that memory, across scales from cells to societies, is best understood as preserving salience (what matters for the agent's future) rather than fidelity to the details of the original data.
quote: Using examples from developmental biology, evolution, and synthetic bioengineering, in addition to neuroscience, I propose that a perspective on memory as preserving salience, not fidelity, is applicable to many phenomena on scales from cells to societies.
scope: Living systems from cells to societies

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Adaptive confabulation resolves the persistence paradox for individuals and lineages
statement: Levin argues that the paradox that a changing agent or species ceases to be itself while an unchanging one dies out is resolved by continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation (reinterpretation of memories and information) at levels from molecular to behavioural, in individuals and whole lineages.
quote: Continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation, from the molecular to the behavioral levels, is the answer to the persistence paradox as it applies to individuals and whole lineages.
scope: Individual organisms and evolutionary lineages

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Memories may be active agents in the sense-making process
statement: Levin speculates that, on a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind, memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as minimally agential participants that help shape their own reinterpretation, blurring the line between thoughts and thinkers.
quote: I also speculate that a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind suggests that memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as active agents in the sense-making process.
scope: Cognitive systems in general

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Reinterpreting non-local memories is a cognitive glue that makes Selves
statement: Levin proposes that mnemonic improvisation, the ability to modify, remap and interpret non-local memories onto new media and contexts, is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that binds parts into a Self at every scale.
quote: Thus, I propose that the ability to modify and interpret non-local memories is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that reifies Selves (at all scales) [23,24,25].
scope: Agents at all scales, from cells to organisms

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Memories surviving metamorphosis are remapped to stay salient in the new body
statement: In insects whose memories survive metamorphosis (caterpillar to butterfly), recall does not carry over specific caterpillar memories but generalizes and remaps them (e.g. from leaves to food) so that the learned relationship keeps its salience in the new body and environment.
quote: The process of memory and recall not only functionally generalizes (abstracts20) the information (not leaves, but “food”), but most importantly, remaps21 it in a way that the basic relationship learned maintains its salience in a new body and environment.
scope: Holometabolous insects (e.g. Lepidoptera) retaining learned associations through metamorphosis

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Engrams act more like prompts decoded by an intelligent receiver than like encodings
statement: From examples such as frogs that seek out an odorant injected into the egg they developed from, Levin argues that engrams behave less like encoded memories and more like prompts, with much of the work (detecting novelty, remapping across scales, contextualizing and generalizing) done by the encoding and decoding process.
quote: The engrams seem less like encoded memories29, and more like a kind of prompt, with a lot of the hard work being carried out through the encoding/decoding process, which adds interpretation, context sensitivity, and generalization (i.e., intelligence) to the process.
scope: Memory transfer phenomena in animals (frog eggs, Aplysia brain-extract transfer)

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: The same bioelectric trigger is reinterpreted by context (monensin: tails vs legs)
statement: Low-information bioelectric triggers are interpreted by competent tissues according to context: the voltage-modifying reagent monensin induces tail regrowth in tadpoles but leg regrowth in froglets, never the reverse, preserving high-level information such as 'build whatever normally goes at this location'.
quote: Here, the same bioelectric stimulus is functionally reinterpreted based on the specific context, preserving salient, high-level information like “build whatever normally goes at this location” (in the case of the appendage regeneration trigger).
scope: Xenopus tadpole tail and froglet hindlimb regeneration

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Polyploid newts build normal tubules by switching molecular mechanisms
statement: Engineered polyploid newts with much larger cells keep kidney tubule diameter normal by using fewer cells and, with truly enormous cells, a single cell bending around itself, showing that tissues call up different molecular mechanisms (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication) to reach the same anatomical goal state.
quote: This requires using a different molecular mechanism (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication of tubulogenesis)—calling up different modular subroutines to accomplish their high-level goal state as needed, while circumstances (indeed, their inner components) change unexpectedly34.
scope: Polyploid newt kidney tubules

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Bowtie compression is common in biochemical, bioelectric and mechanical pathways
statement: Levin argues that a bowtie architecture, which compresses data to a generative kernel that must later be re-inflated and reinterpreted, is common at the subcellular scale in biochemical, bioelectrical and biomechanical pathways, as well as in the egg stage of the metazoan life cycle and in learning.
quote: Note that this bowtie architecture—which forces a compression36 of data to a generative kernel that then has to be re-inflated and elaborated—is also a common feature of biochemical, bioelectrical, and biomechanical pathways (Figure 7), that is, at the subcellular scale;
scope: Subcellular signalling pathways and metazoan life cycles

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Anatomical plasticity across species reflects willingness to confabulate in morphospace
statement: Levin proposes that the spectrum from hardwired, mosaic C. elegans through intermediately plastic amphibians and embryonic mammals to extremely plastic planaria reflects a strategic parameter: the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space, i.e. to rely on pattern extraction and completion rather than taking genetic priors too seriously.
quote: What underlying parameter is represented by the spectrum ranging from the hardwired, mosaic C. elegans to the intermediately plastic amphibia and (embryonic) mammals, and to the extreme plasticity of planaria? I propose it is the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space
scope: Metazoans from C. elegans to amphibians, mammals and planaria

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Planaria resist cancer and ageing despite noisy genomes via pattern completion
statement: In silico simulations show how lineages such as planarian flatworms can become extremely resistant to transgenesis, ageing, cancer and injury despite very noisy genomes because they commit to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion.
quote: In silico simulation results [176] show how this kind of process can give rise to remarkable lineages, such as planarian flatworms, which are extremely resistant to transgenesis, aging, cancer, and injury despite40 their incredibly noisy genome because they have fully committed to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion [176].
scope: Planarian flatworms (e.g. Schmidtea mediterranea) and in silico evolutionary models

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Substrate unreliability is the reason, not an obstacle, for biological intelligence
statement: Levin argues that the noise and unreliability of biological matter is a feature rather than a bug: morphological and behavioural intelligence arose because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate, as suggested by planaria having the noisiest genome and the best regeneration and cancer resistance.
quote: It seems that the underlying noise and unreliability of biological matter is not a bug but a feature: we obtained morphological (and behavioral) intelligence because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate45.
scope: Living organisms, especially metazoans

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Cellular competency hides genome quality from selection, driving an intelligence ratchet
statement: Because competent biological material compensates for defects, selection cannot see genome quality clearly, so more evolutionary change accrues in competency mechanisms than in structural components, producing a positive-feedback intelligence ratchet based on remapping information to new contexts.
quote: The competency of our material means that selection cannot see the quality of genomes clearly46. More evolutionary work thus has to be conducted on the competency mechanisms, not the structural components, leading to a positive feedback loop—an intelligence ratchet based on the remapping of information to new contexts47.
scope: Evolution of multicellular organisms; in silico evolutionary models

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: There is no single substrate for memory; all components can serve as scratchpads
statement: Levin hypothesizes that there is no single substrate for memory: every component of a living system can use everything in its environment, including the high-dimensional reservoir of subcellular structure, as an interpretable scratchpad, rather than engrams residing only in synapses.
quote: My current hypothesis, driven by the above multi-scale perspective [218], is that there is no single substrate for memory49.
scope: Nervous systems and non-neural tissues

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Training associative memories may increase integration of composite systems
statement: Levin proposes that memories belonging to a collective (e.g. a rat's lever–reward association, which no single cell experiences) may help reify the collective Self, and that training associative memories into gene regulatory networks should be tested for increases in integrated information (self-coherence).
quote: This is currently being investigated in the context of our training of associative memories into gene-regulatory networks and other substrates, with measures of integrated information to determine if the forming of memories increases the self-coherence of composite systems.
scope: Gene regulatory network models and other composite systems

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Consciousness may be palpated uncertainty about one's own memories
statement: Extending Solms's idea that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about the outside world, Levin hypothesizes that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about one's own memories and internal states.
quote: I propose to expand this idea, with the hypothesis that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about your own memories and internal states.
scope: Conscious agents

work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
label: Behavioural intelligence evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving
statement: Levin proposes that behavioural intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space, which were themselves required by the inevitability of mutation and injury.
quote: Behavioral intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space [97,124].
scope: Evolution of animals with nervous systems

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Planaria have chaotic genomes yet regenerate, resist cancer and do not age
statement: Planaria, despite chaotic mixoploid genomes from ~400 million years of asexual reproduction and large numbers of plastic proliferative stem cells, are champions of regeneration, cancer resistant and apparently do not age, the opposite of what a 'genome drives function' paradigm would predict.
quote: Despite that, they are champions of regeneration, are cancer resistant, and apparently do not age. This is the polar opposite of the outcome that the current paradigm of “genome drives function” would predict for the animal with the messiest genome, full of undifferentiated cells in the adult stage.
scope: Asexual planarian flatworms (e.g. Schmidtea mediterranea asexual strain)

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: The body is a collective intelligence, so behavioural tools should beat micromanagement
statement: Levin's central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological and transcriptional spaces, so behavioural-science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement of molecular components.
quote: The central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological, and transcriptional spaces [13]. Thus, behavioral science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement.
scope: Human and animal bodies; biomedical and bioengineering interventions

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Intelligence is reaching the same goal by different means, including in morphogenesis
statement: Levin defines intelligence, following William James, as the ability to reach the same goal by different means; for tissues this is the problem-solving competency to adapt to conditions in order to construct and repair a specific morphology or function, a functional definition that lets intelligence be studied in non-neural substrates.
quote: I define intelligence here in William James’ [22] sense as the ability to reach the same goal by different means: the focus is on problem‐solving competency, which in this case is the ability to adapt to conditions to construct and repair a specific morphology or function.
scope: Any biological system, from molecular networks to organisms

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Gene regulatory network models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian learning
statement: When standard behavioural-training protocols are applied to even simple models of gene regulatory networks and molecular pathways, the models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning, a dynamical state memory that requires no change to network topology or edge strengths.
quote: By applying standard approaches from behavioral theory [17], it was seen that even simple models of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and molecular pathways show several different kinds of learning, including habituation, sensitization, and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning [23, 24].
scope: Computational models of gene regulatory networks and molecular pathways (cited work from the author's group, refs [23, 24])

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Planarian heads degenerated by barium regenerate adapted to it via a handful of genes
statement: Planarian flatworms exposed to barium, a nonspecific potassium channel blocker, lose their heads but soon regenerate new heads completely adapted to barium, and transcriptomic analysis shows only a handful of genes up- or down-regulated, which Levin interprets as cells solving a problem in high-dimensional transcriptional space without an evolved response to barium.
quote: Remarkably, they soon regenerate new heads which are completely adapted to the presence of barium [66]. Transcriptomic analysis reveals just a handful of genes that have been up‐ and down‐regulated to enable this feat of morphological and physiological homeostasis.
scope: Planarian flatworms exposed to barium chloride (author's lab's prior work, ref [66])

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Morphogenesis is behaviour of cell collectives navigating anatomical morphospace
statement: Morphogenesis can be viewed as behaviour in anatomical morphospace: cellular collectives actively navigate from various starting states to the region corresponding to the species-specific target morphology, with competency ranging from a constrained random walk to advanced problem-solving, a framing Levin presents as a useful metaphor for importing tools from behavioural and cognitive science.
quote: We previously argued that morphogenesis can be viewed as behavior in anatomical morphospace [13]; on this model, cellular collectives are systems that actively navigate from various starting states to a region corresponding to the species‐specific target morphology (Figure 2).
scope: Developing and regenerating multicellular organisms

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Anatomical homeostasis uses large-scale feedback loops that reduce error from a target
statement: Morphogenetic problem-solving cases indicate that anatomical development is not entirely open-loop: large-scale feedback loops measure distance from a target anatomical state and execute diverse molecular steps to reduce the error, and such networks can store setpoints that are complex data structures rather than simple scalars.
quote: These examples indicate that these processes are not entirely open‐loop: large‐scale feedback loops exist that measure distance from a given target state and execute diverse molecular steps to implement those goals (reduce error).
scope: Regulative development and regeneration in animals (e.g. the cases in the paper's Table 1)

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Channelopathies that cause patterning defects link developmental biology and neuroscience
statement: The deep symmetry between developmental biology and neuroscience is shown by the many ion-channel diseases (channelopathies) that produce patterning defects, and by the applicability of neuroscience tools, from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols, to morphogenetic decisions.
quote: It can be seen in numerous channelopathies that result in patterning defects (see Table 1 in [110], and [111, 112, 113]), and in the applicability of the tools of neuroscience—from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols—to morphogenetic decisions.
scope: Vertebrates including humans; ion channel genes and developmental phenotypes

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: An endogenous electric face of resting potentials determines vertebrate face patterning
statement: An endogenous spatial distribution of resting membrane potentials (the 'electric face') determines gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face; manipulating it by pharmacology, optogenetics or ion channel misexpression predictably changes craniofacial development and explains why ion channel mutations cause craniofacial phenotypes from frog to human.
quote: One example is the electric face (Figure 4B)—an endogenous distribution of resting potentials that determines the gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face [118].
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos, generalized to vertebrates including humans (author's lab's prior work, refs [118, 119])

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: A membrane-voltage change can induce eyes almost anywhere in the Xenopus body
statement: In Xenopus laevis, misexpressing potassium channels to change membrane voltage induces ectopic eyes in many posterior regions including the gut, showing that cells outside the anterior neural field are competent to build eyes when given a higher-level bioelectric signal, contrary to conclusions drawn from prompting cells with the 'master eye gene' Pax6.
quote: It was always thought that cells outside the anterior neural field in vertebrates were not competent to build eyes. But prior studies prompted cells with the so‐called master eye gene Pax6 [123]. It turns out that a higher‐level signal (V mem change) can induce eyes almost anywhere in the body.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos injected with potassium channel mRNA (author's lab's prior work, ref [120])

work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
label: Many ectopic eye spots but one eye reflect competing goals of neighbouring cell groups
statement: In Xenopus embryos injected with a potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots appear early but typically only one new eye forms; Levin interprets this as bidirectional signalling between channel-induced cells pushed toward an eye setpoint, which recruit neighbours, and uninjected neighbours whose setpoint is still 'gut', which signal to maintain normal fate.
quote: At early stages in embryos injected with the potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots are detected, but just one new eye tends to appear at the end. This is the consequence of conversation between morphogenetic agents with different goals.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos misexpressing potassium channels
